question: What's the difference between a writer's voice and a writer's style, and can you have one without the other?
lookingFor: A precise craft distinction rather than treating the two words as interchangeable synonyms.

bullets: Style is the technical choices on the page (syntax, diction, rhythm, punctuation)
Voice is the underlying sensibility or worldview that persists even when style shifts
Give a concrete example of a writer who changes style across books but keeps a recognisable voice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Style is the visible machinery, things like sentence length, punctuation habits, how much white space a writer leaves on the page. Voice is more like the personality underneath that machinery, the particular way someone notices the world, which stays consistent even if the style shifts. Cormac McCarthy writes in very different registers across his books, some sparse and some baroque, but you can still feel the same unflinching, almost biblical attention behind all of them. I think you can fake a style fairly quickly by imitation, but voice is much harder to fake because it comes from how you actually see things.

commonMistakes: Treating voice and style as the same thing
Giving a purely abstract answer with no example
Claiming voice can be taught step by step like a formula
followUps: Whose voice do you think you've absorbed the most, and how do you try to write past that influence?

question: "Show, don't tell" is the most repeated piece of writing advice there is. When is it actually wrong?
lookingFor: Evidence of thinking past workshop cliches and understanding that telling has legitimate uses.

bullets: Acknowledge why the advice exists (immersion, trust in the reader, avoiding melodrama)
Give a specific case where telling is the better craft choice, such as compressing time or controlling pace
Show awareness that skilled writers deliberately break the rule for effect
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It exists because beginning writers tend to announce emotions instead of earning them, so showing forces you to trust the reader with detail instead of a label. But if you showed every single moment in full scene, a novel would take forever to get anywhere, so telling is often exactly right for compressing time, like summarising three uneventful years in a sentence so the important scene can breathe. Some of my favourite lines are flatly told rather than shown, because the bluntness itself creates a tone. I think the real rule is closer to know why you're choosing one or the other, not always show.

commonMistakes: Reciting the rule without questioning it
Rejecting the advice entirely with no acknowledgment of its purpose
Giving no concrete example of successful telling
followUps: Can you think of a moment in your own writing where you chose to tell rather than show, and why?

question: How does a writer make a first-person narrator unreliable without the reader feeling cheated by the twist?
lookingFor: Understanding of fair-play technique, that unreliability should be seeded through gaps or contradictions, not concealed until a reveal.

bullets: Explain that the trick is planting small inconsistencies or gaps the reader can notice on a second read
Distinguish a fair unreliable narrator from one that withholds information the narrator themselves would know
Reference or invent a concrete technique, like other characters' reactions contradicting the narrator's account
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the reader has to feel like they had a fair shot at seeing it, so the writer needs to leave small cracks early on, a detail that doesn't quite match what the narrator claims, or another character reacting oddly to something the narrator described as ordinary. What feels cheap is when the narrator hides a fact they obviously knew the whole time purely for a twist, because that's withholding rather than unreliability. Nabokov does this brilliantly in Lolita, where Humbert's own language keeps betraying him even as he tries to charm the reader into sympathy. The unreliability has to come from character, from what the narrator needs to believe about themselves, not just from the plot needing a surprise.

commonMistakes: Describing unreliable narration as simply lying to the reader
Confusing unreliable narration with an unlikeable narrator
No mention of fairness or seeding clues
followUps: Have you tried writing an unreliable narrator yourself? What went wrong the first time?

question: Walk us through how you'd revise a short story after finishing a first draft. What do you look at first?
lookingFor: A concrete, staged revision process, showing the applicant treats drafting and revising as distinct disciplines.

bullets: Describe letting the draft sit before returning to it
Prioritise structural and character-level issues before line-level polishing
Mention a specific technique, like reading aloud or tracking a character's wants scene by scene
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I try to leave a first draft alone for at least a week so I stop remembering what I meant to write and can actually see what's on the page. Then I read the whole thing straight through without fixing anything, just noting where I get bored or confused, because those spots usually point to a structural problem rather than a sentence problem. Only after I've sorted out whether the story's shape actually works do I go line by line, and I always read the dialogue aloud because clunky rhythm is much easier to hear than to see. Fixing commas before fixing the ending has burned me before, so I try to work big to small.

commonMistakes: Describing revision as just fixing typos and grammar
No sense of sequencing, jumping straight to line edits
Vague answer with no concrete method
followUps: What's a piece of your own writing you revised so heavily it became almost a different story?

question: How does reading as a writer differ from reading as a regular reader? Give us an example from something you've read recently.
lookingFor: Evidence of analytical, craft-focused reading habits rather than only summarising plot or theme.

bullets: Distinguish reading for enjoyment or plot from reading to notice technique
Give a specific, recent text and a specific technical observation from it
Show that this analytical reading actually feeds back into their own writing
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As a reader I want to know what happens next, but as a writer I keep stopping to ask how the author made me feel that, which slows me right down and sometimes ruins the momentum of a good thriller. Reading Jenny Offill's Dept. of Speculation recently, I kept noticing how she uses white space and fragmented paragraphs to mimic a mind under strain, and I actually went back and counted how short some of her paragraphs were. It made me try the same fragmentation in a piece about insomnia I was struggling with, because straight prose wasn't capturing the disjointed feeling I wanted. So reading as a writer is a bit like reading with the hood up, looking at the engine instead of just enjoying the drive.

commonMistakes: Naming a book with no specific craft observation
Only summarising the plot or theme
Claiming to read purely for pleasure with no analytical habit
followUps: What's a technique from that book you'd be nervous to try yourself, and why?

question: A workshop peer tells you your protagonist is unlikeable and that's a problem. How do you respond to that critique?
lookingFor: Ability to separate useful craft feedback from taste-based feedback, without dismissing critique defensively.

bullets: Distinguish unlikeable from unconvincing or uninteresting, since likeability is not always the goal
Show willingness to interrogate whether the character is actually working, not just defend the choice
Land on a considered response rather than either capitulating entirely or dismissing the note
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: My first instinct would be to ask what specifically made them feel that way, because unlikeable and poorly written are not the same problem, and plenty of great fiction has deliberately unlikeable narrators. If the note is really that the character feels unlikeable in a way that isn't earning the reader's attention, that's worth taking seriously, but if the note is just that the character made a choice the reader disagreed with, I'd probably hold my ground. I try to treat workshop feedback as data about how the piece landed rather than instructions to follow automatically, so I'd weigh it against what I was actually trying to do with that character.

commonMistakes: Getting defensive and dismissing the feedback outright
Agreeing immediately with no independent judgment
Not distinguishing likeable from compelling
followUps: Tell us about a time feedback changed your mind about a piece you were attached to.

question: What can a poem do that a short story can't, and vice versa?
lookingFor: Genuine comparative understanding of form, not just a preference statement.

bullets: Identify something specific to poetry's compression, sound, or line breaks
Identify something specific to prose's capacity for sustained narrative or interiority over time
Avoid treating one form as simply harder or more serious than the other
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A poem can hold a single moment under so much pressure that a line break or a sound pattern does work a whole paragraph of prose might need to do, it can suspend time in a way prose usually can't afford to. A short story, on the other hand, can let a character's understanding of something change gradually across scenes, which needs duration that a poem's compression tends to resist. I don't think one is harder than the other, they're just solving different problems, poetry is closer to a single held breath and prose is closer to a walk.

commonMistakes: Vague claim that poetry is 'more emotional' with no craft reasoning
Implying one form is inherently superior
No specific technical distinction offered
followUps: Have you ever taken a poem and tried turning it into prose, or the reverse? What happened?

question: Do you believe in writing every day, or do you think that advice is overrated?
lookingFor: A self-aware, specific account of the applicant's actual process, not a recitation of famous writers' routines.

bullets: Give an honest account of their own current habits, not an idealised version
Show awareness that different stages of a project might need different rhythms
Avoid treating a single routine as the universally correct one
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I used to think I had to write every single day or I wasn't a real writer, but that just made me dread sitting down, so now I aim for most days and give myself real permission to skip a day if I'm still turning something over in my head. What I've noticed is that drafting needs frequency to keep momentum, but revising works better for me in longer, less frequent stretches where I can hold the whole piece in mind. I don't think there's one correct routine, I think the goal is figuring out what your own brain actually needs at each stage.

commonMistakes: Reciting a famous author's routine with no personal reflection
Claiming a rigid daily habit that sounds performative
Dismissing routine entirely as unnecessary
followUps: What does a bad writing day look like for you, and what do you do about it?

question: Is the line between 'genre fiction' and 'literary fiction' a meaningful distinction, or mostly a marketing category?
lookingFor: A nuanced, opinionated position that engages with both craft and publishing realities rather than a dismissive one-liner.

bullets: Acknowledge the marketing and gatekeeping function of the label
Also grant that certain craft tendencies do cluster differently across the categories
Use a specific example of a book that troubles the distinction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think it's real in the sense that certain conventions genuinely differ, genre fiction often prioritises plot momentum and a satisfying resolution to specific reader expectations, while what gets called literary fiction is often more willing to leave things unresolved or foreground language for its own sake. But a huge amount of that distinction is also just publishing strategy and prestige, deciding which shelf and which prize category a book gets, and it has a history of undervaluing writers of colour and women writing genre. Something like Station Eleven gets shelved as literary despite being a pandemic novel with plenty of genre DNA, which tells you the label is doing some sorting that isn't purely about craft.

commonMistakes: Dismissing the whole question as 'just marketing' with no nuance
Treating literary fiction as automatically superior
No concrete book example to ground the argument
followUps: Where would you place your own writing on that spectrum, and are you comfortable with that?

question: How do you decide what point of view to write a story in? Has a piece of yours ever needed a different POV than the one you started with?
lookingFor: Practical craft reasoning about point of view as a decision with consequences, ideally grounded in the applicant's own experience.

bullets: Connect POV choice to what the story needs, intimacy, distance, or dramatic irony
Give a real or plausible example of a piece that required switching POV
Show understanding of the trade-offs of different POV choices
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I usually think about how close I need the reader to be to one character's thinking, first person gives you total intimacy but limits you to what that character notices, while third limited lets you step back a little without losing interiority entirely. I wrote a story from a mother's first person point of view and it felt suffocating because the story actually needed the reader to see the daughter's absence more clearly than the mother herself could admit, so I switched to third limited on the mother and it opened the story up. It taught me that POV isn't just a stylistic preference, it's basically deciding what the reader is allowed to know.

commonMistakes: Treating POV as an arbitrary stylistic preference with no craft rationale
No specific example from their own writing
Confusing point of view with tense
followUps: What's a story you've read where the POV choice surprised you or felt risky?

question: You want to write a personal essay that includes a painful, true story about a family member who would be recognisable and who hasn't consented to being written about. Do you publish it?
lookingFor: Structured ethical reasoning weighing artistic honesty against the real harm and consent of people who didn't choose to be written about.

bullets: Acknowledge the genuine tension between truth-telling and a real person's right to privacy or dignity
Consider concrete mitigations, such as changing identifying details, sharing the draft with them, or examining whether the story needs that specific person named
Reach a considered position rather than an absolute rule in either direction
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think there's a clean rule here, because the instinct that my story is mine to tell is true, but so is the fact that another person's life becomes material without their say in it. I'd start by asking whether the essay actually needs that person recognisable, or whether I could change enough detail to protect them while keeping the emotional truth intact. If it still needed to be specific, I think I'd owe them the chance to read it before publication, not for a veto necessarily, but so I'm not blindsiding someone I care about. I'd rather risk a slightly less sharp essay than one that costs a real relationship without the other person ever getting a say.

commonMistakes: Claiming absolute artistic freedom with no regard for the subject's harm
Refusing to ever write anything true and difficult about real people
Giving no concrete mitigation, just abstract hand wringing
followUps: Does your answer change if the story reflects badly on you rather than on them?

question: What responsibilities, if any, does a writer have when writing a character from a background very different from their own?
lookingFor: Balanced reasoning that neither forbids writing outside one's identity nor treats it as consequence-free, with awareness of research and craft as the real work.

bullets: Reject both extremes: total prohibition and total entitlement to write anyone
Emphasise specific practices like research, sensitivity readers, or listening rather than assuming
Distinguish careless stereotype from careful, well-researched imagination
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think fiction survives if writers are only allowed to write people exactly like themselves, imagination has to be able to cross that line or the whole project falls apart. But I also think the responsibility is real, it's on the writer to do the actual work, research, listening, sometimes having a sensitivity reader from that background look at the draft, rather than assuming lived proximity to a stereotype is enough. What actually causes harm usually isn't the crossing itself, it's laziness, reaching for a shortcut instead of specificity. So I'd rather ask whether I've earned the portrayal through care than whether I'm technically allowed to attempt it.

commonMistakes: Claiming writers should never write outside their own identity
Claiming total entitlement with no acknowledgment of risk or harm
No mention of concrete practices like research or sensitivity reading
followUps: Have you ever written a character from a very different background, and what did you do to prepare?

question: Where's the line between being heavily influenced by a writer and plagiarising them?
lookingFor: Nuanced understanding of intertextuality, influence, and originality, rather than a naive claim that all writing must be fully original.

bullets: Distinguish surface-level copying (specific sentences, structures, exact plot) from absorbing technique or sensibility
Acknowledge that all writers work within a tradition of influence, including deliberate homage or allusion
Give a concrete boundary, like copying language versus copying a device or approach
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think influence is unavoidable and honestly a good sign, if a piece shows no trace of what you've read it probably means you haven't read enough. The line for me is whether you're copying the actual language or specific invented details versus absorbing a technique, like a way of handling time or dialogue, and then using it on your own material. Homage is usually visible and intentional, you're gesturing at the source, whereas plagiarism tries to hide the debt and pass someone else's specific sentences or plot off as new. I try to ask myself if I could show the original writer my draft without it feeling like I owe them an apology.

commonMistakes: Claiming complete originality is possible or required
No concrete distinction between technique and language
Treating any similarity at all as plagiarism
followUps: Which writer's influence would be most obvious to someone reading your own work?

question: A workshop peer asks that violent or traumatic content in student work come with a warning before it's read aloud. Some classmates think that undermines artistic freedom. Where do you land?
lookingFor: Ability to hold both artistic freedom and reader wellbeing as legitimate concerns and find a workable middle ground.

bullets: Acknowledge the legitimate value on both sides, artistic freedom and real risk of harm to readers
Note that a warning does not censor content, it just changes how it's delivered
Land on a practical, specific position rather than an abstract stance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I don't think a warning stops anyone from writing whatever they want to write, it just gives the room a second to brace before something difficult lands, which seems like basic consideration rather than censorship. At the same time I understand the worry that this could slide into people softening their work to avoid needing a warning at all, which would be a real loss. My actual position is that a short heads up costs the writer almost nothing and can meaningfully help someone in the room who has a real history with that material, so I'd be in favour of it as a workshop norm rather than a rule about content itself.

commonMistakes: Framing any warning as automatic censorship
Dismissing the concern about reader wellbeing entirely
Refusing to take a position at all
followUps: Would your view change if the warning requirement came with an actual restriction on content, not just a heads up?

question: Would you be comfortable ghostwriting a memoir for someone else and having their name alone on the cover? Why or why not?
lookingFor: Thoughtful reflection on authorship, credit, and the practical realities of the writing industry, not a reflexive yes or no.

bullets: Weigh the craft value and financial reality of ghostwriting against the desire for personal authorship credit
Show understanding that ghostwriting is a real, common part of the industry with its own ethics norms, like contracts and disclosure
Reach a genuine personal position rather than a purely diplomatic non-answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think I could do it, and honestly it would be excellent training, capturing someone else's voice accurately is a serious craft skill, arguably harder than writing in your own. What would matter to me is that it's an honest arrangement, the person actually knows and agrees that a ghostwriter is doing the work, rather than the reader being deceived about who wrote the sentences. I'd want fair payment and probably an acknowledgment somewhere even if my name isn't on the spine. I don't think it would feel like a compromise of my own writing as long as I was also making time for work that was fully mine.

commonMistakes: Refusing outright with no engagement with the industry realities
Accepting with no consideration of fairness or disclosure
Confusing ghostwriting with plagiarism
followUps: How would you feel if a piece of your own unpublished writing were later published under someone else's name?

question: AI tools can now generate competent short fiction in seconds. What do you think that means for someone choosing to study creative writing right now?
lookingFor: Genuine, informed engagement with a live debate in the field, avoiding both dismissiveness and panic, grounded in what writing actually requires.

bullets: Show awareness of the actual current state of AI-generated fiction, not an exaggerated or naive picture
Identify something specific writing still requires that generation alone doesn't provide, like lived judgment, revision taste, or intention
Give a genuine, considered opinion rather than a rehearsed reassurance
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've actually tried getting AI tools to write fiction, and what strikes me is that they're often competent at the sentence level but they don't have anything at stake, there's no accumulated experience pushing a particular story to exist. What a writer brings that generation doesn't is judgment, knowing which of a hundred competent sentences is actually the right one for this story, and that comes from taste built over years of reading and writing badly first. I think it does change the job market for certain kinds of formulaic commercial writing, and I'm not going to pretend that's not unsettling, but it makes the case for training as a writer stronger to me, not weaker, because the judgment is the actual scarce skill.

commonMistakes: Dismissing AI as irrelevant with no real engagement
Sounding panicked with no concrete reasoning about what writers still uniquely offer
Giving an answer that shows no firsthand familiarity with the tools
followUps: Have you used any AI writing tools yourself, and what did that experience actually teach you?

question: There's an ongoing debate about whether formal creative writing programs actually help writers or just homogenise them. What's your take?
lookingFor: Awareness of a real, ongoing debate in the field, with a considered position rather than blind faith in the institution they're applying to.

bullets: Show awareness of the actual critique, that workshops can push writing toward a similar polished, risk-averse style
Weigh that against genuine benefits, structured feedback, deadlines, a community of serious readers
Give a personal, specific reason this program still makes sense for them despite the critique
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think the criticism has real substance, workshop culture can quietly reward a certain kind of tidy, well-behaved story and make writers flinch away from riskier choices because a room full of peers is giving live feedback. But I don't think that's inevitable, it depends a lot on the specific program and how much risk-taking is actually encouraged versus just competence. What I want from a program isn't to be told the right way to write, it's structured time, serious readers, and enough deadline pressure that I actually finish things instead of endlessly tinkering alone. I'm going in aware of the homogenising risk, which is partly why I looked for a program that seemed to value range over a house style.

commonMistakes: No awareness that this critique exists at all
Uncritical praise of formal programs with no acknowledgment of drawbacks
Dismissing programs entirely, which undercuts their own application
followUps: What would you do if you felt your own voice was being smoothed out by workshop feedback?

question: Autofiction, writing that blurs memoir and fiction, has been one of the biggest trends in literary writing over the last decade. What do you think is driving that, and does it interest you?
lookingFor: Awareness of a specific, current literary trend with an informed opinion, ideally naming relevant writers or works.

bullets: Name the trend accurately and reference at least one relevant writer or work
Offer a plausible explanation for its popularity, such as distrust of the omniscient narrator or the pull of authenticity culture
Give a genuine personal reaction, whether drawn to it or skeptical of it
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Writers like Rachel Cusk and Karl Ove Knausgaard are the obvious reference points, work that refuses to hide the seam between the author's actual life and the narrator's. I think part of what's driving it is a kind of fatigue with the traditional omniscient, plotted novel, and part of it is a culture that's generally hungry for a feeling of authenticity, even when that authenticity is itself carefully constructed. I find it genuinely interesting but also a little suspicious of itself, because claiming closeness to real life is its own kind of performance, and I'd want to write something that's honest about that tension rather than pretending the memoir label makes it more true.

commonMistakes: Unable to name a relevant writer or example
Confusing autofiction with straightforward memoir
Giving no personal opinion, only a neutral definition
followUps: Would you ever write autofiction about your own life? What would hold you back?

question: Self-publishing and platforms like Substack are letting writers reach readers without traditional publishers. Does that change how you think about a writing career?
lookingFor: Practical awareness of the current publishing landscape and its trade-offs, not idealised naivety about either path.

bullets: Show awareness of specific trade-offs, like editorial support and reach versus creative control and speed
Avoid treating either traditional publishing or self-publishing as automatically superior
Connect it to their own realistic sense of what kind of career they want
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: It definitely changes the picture, a writer building an audience directly on Substack has a kind of control and immediacy that traditional publishing timelines just don't allow, sometimes a book takes two years to reach readers after it's finished. But I don't think it replaces what a good editor and a publisher's distribution and credibility can do, especially early on when you don't yet have an audience to build from. I'd actually like to try both, maybe building a small following with essays or serialised fiction online while also aiming for traditional publication for longer work, rather than treating it as an either or choice.

commonMistakes: Dismissing self-publishing as inherently lesser
Claiming traditional publishing is obsolete
No awareness of concrete trade-offs, just vague enthusiasm
followUps: Have you ever published anything yourself, even informally, and what did you learn from readers' reactions?

question: If you had to write an entire short story without using the letter 'e', the way Georges Perec wrote a whole novel that way, what would change about how you approached the story, beyond just word choice?
lookingFor: Genuine engagement with constraint-based writing as a creative tool, showing understanding that constraints reshape more than vocabulary.

bullets: Show awareness that a constraint like this forces structural and even plot-level changes, not just synonym swapping
Reflect on what kind of story or voice might actually suit that constraint
Show genuine curiosity or specific reasoning rather than treating it as a gimmick
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The first thing that would go is a huge amount of ordinary vocabulary, no 'the', no 'she', no 'he', so I'd probably end up writing in a strange clipped register almost by necessity, which might actually suit a story about someone who's lost the ability to speak normally, so the constraint becomes the theme instead of fighting against it. I think I'd stop trying to write my usual sentences and translate them, and instead let the missing letter dictate the plot itself, maybe a character obsessively avoiding something. It would be exhausting, but I think that kind of constraint is useful precisely because it breaks your habitual phrasing and forces genuinely new choices.

commonMistakes: Treating it as purely a vocabulary puzzle with no structural thinking
Refusing to engage seriously with the hypothetical
No awareness of the real precedent (Perec's La Disparition) or similar constrained writing
followUps: What's a constraint you've actually tried in your own writing, even something small like a word limit?

question: Imagine you've written a short story for adults, but a publisher offers to buy it only if you rework it for a children's audience. What would actually have to change, and what would you refuse to change?
lookingFor: Concrete craft thinking about how audience shapes content, structure and language, plus a sense of the applicant's own creative boundaries.

bullets: Identify specific things that would need to change, such as vocabulary, pacing, explicit content, or moral clarity
Identify something they would protect, like the emotional core or a difficult truth
Show they understand rewriting for audience is a real craft skill, not just simplification
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A lot would have to change beyond vocabulary, the pacing would need to move faster, explicit or graphic moments would need to happen off the page, and the story would probably need a clearer emotional throughline since younger readers are less patient with ambiguity. What I'd refuse to simplify is the actual emotional truth, children's fiction handles hard things like grief or fear all the time, it just does it with more trust in the reader's imagination rather than less honesty. I think the mistake would be assuming younger readers need things dumbed down rather than just told differently, so I'd try to protect the feeling of the story even while the plot mechanics changed a lot.

commonMistakes: Assuming rewriting for children just means removing bad words
Refusing to change anything at all, missing the actual craft challenge
Losing the emotional core entirely in the process of simplifying
followUps: What's a children's book you think handles a genuinely difficult theme well?

question: How would you give feedback on a classmate's story that you think has a strong premise but doesn't work at all on the page?
lookingFor: Constructive, specific critique technique that separates the writer's intention from the execution, rather than vague praise or vague criticism.

bullets: Start by identifying and naming what the story is trying to do, not just what's wrong
Give specific, actionable observations rather than general impressions
Balance honesty with respect for the writer's ownership of the piece
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd start by telling them what I think the story is actually reaching for, because naming that shows I read it carefully and it gives us a shared target to talk about. Then I'd try to be specific rather than just saying it doesn't work, maybe pointing out that the opening scene doesn't establish stakes fast enough, or that a key relationship isn't earned before an important choice happens. I try to frame notes as questions when I can, like asking what the character wants in this scene, because it invites the writer to solve it themselves rather than me rewriting their story for them. The goal is that they leave the conversation excited to revise, not defensive.

commonMistakes: Giving only vague praise with no actionable notes
Being harshly critical with no acknowledgment of what's working
Rewriting the story in their head instead of respecting the writer's intent
followUps: How do you handle it when a writer pushes back on feedback you feel strongly about?

question: What makes dialogue on the page feel real, given that real speech is actually full of filler and repetition that would be unreadable if transcribed exactly?
lookingFor: Understanding that good dialogue is a stylised illusion of speech, not a literal transcript, with an eye for subtext.

bullets: Note that real transcribed speech is full of filler that would bore a reader
Identify that good dialogue compresses and shapes speech while keeping its rhythm and personality
Mention subtext, that what characters don't say is often as important as what they do
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If you actually transcribed how people talk, it's full of half sentences, ums, and people talking past each other, and on the page that just reads as clutter rather than realism. What makes dialogue feel real is usually rhythm and personality rather than literal accuracy, keeping each character's particular way of dodging a question or interrupting, while cutting out the filler that doesn't earn its place. I think the best dialogue is also doing two things at once, there's the actual words and then there's what the character is avoiding saying, and that gap is usually where the tension lives.

commonMistakes: Believing dialogue should mimic real transcribed speech exactly
Writing dialogue that's purely functional with no character distinction
No mention of subtext or what's left unsaid
followUps: Can you think of a line of dialogue you've written where what's unsaid mattered more than what was said?

question: When does a nonlinear structure actually serve a story, versus just being a stylistic trick to disguise a weak plot?
lookingFor: Sophisticated understanding of structure as a meaning-making choice, not decoration, with a specific example.

bullets: Articulate a reason nonlinearity can be earned, such as mirroring memory, trauma, or how understanding actually unfolds
Identify the failure mode, using it to hide a lack of forward momentum or tension
Reference a specific book or film that uses nonlinear structure well
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think nonlinear structure earns its place when the order of information is doing real work, like when a story about grief jumps around the way memory actually does, circling a loss instead of marching through it chronologically. It becomes a trick when a fairly straightforward story is chopped up just to seem more literary or to hide that not much is actually happening once you put it back in order. Jennifer Egan's A Visit from the Goon Squad moves around in time and voice constantly, but each jump reveals something about how the characters' pasts keep shaping who they became, so the structure is doing thematic work, not just decoration. I try to ask myself if I could tell the story chronologically and lose something essential, and if the answer is no, the nonlinearity probably isn't earning its keep.

commonMistakes: Treating nonlinear structure as automatically more sophisticated
No example of a story that uses it well
Unable to articulate the failure mode where it's used as decoration
followUps: Have you ever written something nonlinear? Did it actually need to be?

question: What makes an ending feel earned rather than either too neat or frustratingly unresolved?
lookingFor: Nuanced understanding of ending craft, connecting resolution to what the story actually promised earlier, rather than a formula.

bullets: Connect a satisfying ending to whether it answers the question the story actually raised, not necessarily every plot thread
Distinguish earned ambiguity from simply failing to commit to an ending
Give a concrete example of an ending they admired or one that disappointed them
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think an ending feels earned when it answers the actual question the story was quietly asking, which isn't always the same as tying up every plot thread. A story can end ambiguously and still feel complete if the ambiguity itself is the point, like it's honest about a question that doesn't have a clean answer, but that's different from an ending that just trails off because the writer didn't know how to land it. The ending of Kazuo Ishiguro's Never Let Me Go doesn't resolve the injustice at the heart of the book, but it doesn't need to, because the story was never asking whether the characters would escape, it was asking how someone makes peace with a fate they can't change. When an ending disappoints me it's usually because it answers a question the story was never actually asking.

commonMistakes: Assuming a satisfying ending always means a tidy, fully resolved one
